summary: Defines metrics for measuring connectivity between a pair of Internet hosts. It replaced RFC 2498.

eli5.summary: Rules for checking whether one computer can reach another, so measurements agree.

questions: how many probe packets for connectivity test
subtitle: Precise definitions of what it means for two Internet hosts to be connected, and a way to estimate it.

tldr.problem: Measuring whether Internet hosts can reach each other needs exact definitions, otherwise different tools report different things.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a chain of Boolean metrics, from one-way connectivity at an instant to two-way temporal connectivity over an interval, and sketches a probing method to estimate the last one.
tldr.outcome: It is the base of the IPPM measurement suite and obsoletes RFC 2498. It warns that active probing can be abused for denial-of-service attacks.

today: RFC 2678 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1999. It obsoletes RFC 2498, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Connectivity as a Measurable Thing
sections.content:
The RFC argues that connectivity is the basic stuff the Internet is made from, so metrics saying whether pairs of hosts (IP addresses) can reach each other must form the base of a measurement suite. It builds on the IPPM framework in RFC 2330, and assumes the reader knows it.

The memo builds up in steps: one-way connectivity at one moment, then two-way at one moment, then both over an interval, then a useful two-way notion called Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity, and finally methodologies to estimate it. The RFC names the careful definition of that last metric and the discussion of its methodologies as its two chief contributions. All of its metrics are Boolean.
sections.eli5: To check whether two friends can pass notes, you first have to decide exactly what counts as passing a note. This document does that.

sections.title: Instantaneous Connectivity
sections.content:
Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity takes a source address, a destination address and a time T. Src has it to Dst at time T if a type-P packet sent from Src to Dst at time T will arrive at Dst.

The RFC notes that most applications, such as a TCP connection, need two-way connectivity over an interval, though one-way and instantaneous connectivity can matter for security uses such as testing whether a firewall filters a "ping of death". It also does not define when the packet must arrive. The IP TTL is meant to limit lifetimes to 255 seconds, though in practice it can be a hop count, so packet lifetimes must be considered when measuring.

Type-P-Instantaneous-Bidirectional-Connectivity holds for addresses A1 and A2 at time T if each has the one-way metric to the other. The RFC mentions an alternative definition that lets A2's reply travel after A1's packet arrives, which is easier to measure but breaks the symmetry, and postpones it to the interval metrics.
sections.eli5: Instant connectivity asks: if I throw a ball right now, will it land in your hands? Two-way asks if both of us could catch right now.

sections.title: Connectivity Over an Interval
sections.content:
Real applications need connectivity over a stretch of time, and an instant can fail because of a transient event such as a full router queue. The interval metrics add a duration dT, giving the closed interval [T, T+dT].

Type-P-Interval-Unidirectional-Connectivity holds if for some T' within the interval, Src has instantaneous connectivity to Dst. Type-P-Interval-Bidirectional-Connectivity holds if each address has the one-way interval metric to the other during the interval.

The RFC admits this two-way version is not quite what is needed. The two directions might work only at different times, for example early in the interval, so that neither side could reply to the other. That deficiency motivates the next metric.
sections.eli5: Over an interval you ask if the ball can land at least once during a whole afternoon. But it might land only in the morning, too early for you to throw one back.

sections.title: Two-way Temporal Connectivity
sections.content:
Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity is the metric the RFC treats as "generally useful": Src can send a packet to Dst that elicits a response. Its parameters are Src, Dst, T and dT.

It holds if there are times T1 and T2, and delays dT1 and dT2, such that T1, T1+dT1, T2 and T2+dT2 all lie within [T, T+dT], T1+dT1 is no later than T2, Src has Type-P1 instantaneous connectivity to Dst at T1, and Dst has Type-P2 instantaneous connectivity to Src at T2. dT1 and dT2 are the transit times of the two packets.

The forward and reverse packets may be different types, because applications often use different packet types in each direction and the wanted reply to a Type-P1 packet is likely a different Type-P2.
sections.eli5: This asks the useful question: can I send you something and get an answer back, within the time window, with your answer sent after mine arrives?

sections.title: Estimating the Metric
sections.content:
The RFC sketches a class of methodologies rather than one, since details depend on types P1 and P2. Inputs are the types, the two addresses, the interval, N (the number of probe packets) and W (the waiting time, bounding how long a reply is useful). It requires W <= 255 and dT > W. Recommended values are dT = 60 seconds, W = 10 seconds and N = 20 packets.

The algorithm picks N sending times randomly and uniformly over [T, T+dT-W] and sends a well-formed P1 packet to A2 at each one. A1 watches incoming traffic for a successful reply. Any such reply makes the result true and ends the measurement. If none arrives by T+dT, the result is false.

The RFC calls this inexact, since it cannot probe every instant. N trades precision against network load, and it says the state of the art offers no solid guidance for choosing N, so the values are only guidelines.
sections.eli5: You tap on the door a handful of times at random moments during a minute. If anyone ever answers, the answer is yes. If nobody does, it is no.

sections.title: A TCP Methodology
sections.content:
A TCP-port-N1-port-N2 methodology sends TCP SYN packets from source port N1 to destination port N2 at A2, and interprets what comes back at A1.

  • A SYN-ack with the proper acknowledgement fields and ports means temporal connectivity, so the measurement ends with true.
  • A RST with the proper ports also means temporal connectivity, but a lack of service connectivity for that port pair.
  • An ICMP port-unreachable from A2 likewise means temporal connectivity and no service connectivity.
  • An ICMP host-unreachable or network-unreachable (not necessarily from A2) with a matching enclosed IP header only suggests a lack of connectivity. If no evidence of connectivity appears by T+dT, it can add support to a false result.

If a full connection is accidentally established, the RFC says to tear it down with the usual FIN handshake rather than a RST, since RST packets are not reliably delivered. It adds that using the host's own TCP stack complicates the method because the stack may retransmit the SYN and change the number of probes. Similar methods are said to be needed for ICMP Echo and UDP.
sections.eli5: Knock on a door. If someone says come in, or even if they say go away, you know someone is home. A silent street with a sign saying the road is closed suggests nobody is reachable.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: As RFC 2330 notes, active measurement techniques like these can be abused for denial-of-service attacks disguised as legitimate measurement. The RFC adds that testing for connectivity can be used to probe firewalls and other security mechanisms for weak spots.
sections.eli5: Checking over and over whether a door is open can be a trick to annoy the house or find a weak lock, so it must be done carefully.
